title: Diversity of organisms
summary: What a species is and how we name it, why species can be hard to tell apart, and how chromosomes, karyograms and genomes reveal both the unity and the diversity of life.

keyterms.definition: Differences between organisms, both between and within species; a defining feature of life.
Defining species as groups of organisms with shared observable traits, as used by Linnaeus.
Two-part scientific name: genus (capital initial) then species (lower case), italicised or underlined, e.g. Homo sapiens.
A species is a group of organisms that can actually or potentially interbreed in nature to produce fertile offspring.
A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
The number and type of chromosomes in the nucleus of an organism's cells.
An image of an organism's chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs by length, centromere position and banding pattern.
The constricted region of a chromosome; its position is used to identify chromosomes in a karyogram.
All the genetic information of an organism, including all of its DNA.
A position in a gene or genome where a single base differs between individuals of a species.
Determining the complete base sequence of an organism's genome; used in research on evolution and in personalised medicine.
Transfer of genes between organisms other than from parent to offspring, e.g. plasmids passed between bacteria.
An identification tool consisting of a series of paired choices, each leading to another pair or to a name.
DNA shed by organisms into their environment, e.g. into water or soil, that can be sampled to detect species present.
A short, standardised DNA sequence that differs between species and is used to identify them.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to write the binomial name of humans?
options: Homo Sapiens
homo sapiens
Homo sapiens
Sapiens homo
questions.explanation: The genus has a capital initial, the species name is all lower case, and the name is italicised (or underlined when handwritten).

questions.text: In a binomial name, the first part is the ___.
questions.explanation: The first name is the genus and the second is the specific name; together they identify the species.

questions.prompt: According to the biological species concept, what is a species?
options: A group of organisms that look the same
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
A group of organisms that live in the same habitat
A group of organisms with identical DNA
questions.explanation: Interbreeding to produce fertile offspring is the key criterion. Looking similar is the morphological concept, and members of a species do not have identical DNA.

questions.statement: A horse and a donkey are the same species because they can mate and produce offspring.
questions.explanation: Their offspring, the mule, is sterile. The biological species concept requires fertile offspring, so horses and donkeys are separate species.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

pairs.right: Same species, same area, same time

questions.explanation: Linnaeus classified species by morphology; the biological species concept uses interbreeding; a population is a local group of one species.

questions.prompt: Why is it sometimes difficult to decide whether two populations are separate species?
options: Because speciation is gradual, so diverging populations pass through stages where they are only partly distinct
Because all populations can interbreed
Because species never change over time
Because organisms in different populations always look identical
questions.explanation: When populations stop interbreeding they diverge gradually. Partway through, there is no clear point at which they become separate species.

questions.statement: Variation between organisms is a defining feature of life.
questions.explanation: No two organisms are identical; variation exists both between species and between individuals within a species, and it is the raw material for evolution.

questions.text: A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time is a ___.
questions.explanation: A community includes all species in an area; a population includes only one species.

questions.prompt: Which is a limitation of the morphological species concept?
options: It requires DNA sequencing
It can only be used on fossils
It cannot be applied to plants
Members of one species can look very different, while different species can look alike
questions.explanation: Males and females, or different life stages, may differ greatly, while unrelated species may converge in appearance, so appearance alone can mislead.

questions.prompt: Order the stages as one species splits into two.
items: Population divided so the groups stop interbreeding
Groups gradually diverge in their traits
Groups can no longer interbreed: two species
questions.explanation: Divergence is gradual after interbreeding stops, which is why it is hard to define exactly when separate species exist.

questions.prompt: How are chromosomes arranged in a karyogram?
options: Randomly, as they appeared in the cell
In homologous pairs, by length, centromere position and banding pattern
By the number of genes they carry, alphabetically
Sex chromosomes first, then autosomes from smallest to largest
questions.explanation: Homologous pairs are identified and ordered by decreasing length, with centromere position and banding pattern used to match them; sex chromosomes are placed last.

questions.statement: Humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48.
questions.explanation: Diploid chromosome numbers vary between species: humans have 46 (23 pairs) and chimpanzees 48 (24 pairs).

questions.prompt: Which evidence supports the hypothesis that human chromosome 2 arose by fusion of two ancestral chromosomes?
options: Chromosome 2 is the smallest human chromosome
Chromosome 2 has no genes
Chromosome 2 has telomere sequences near its middle and a second, inactive centromere
Chromosome 2 is only found in females
questions.explanation: Telomere repeats normally only occur at chromosome ends, and a vestigial centromere exists; banding patterns also match two chimpanzee chromosomes.

questions.text: All the genetic information of an organism is its ___.
questions.explanation: The genome is the whole of an organism's DNA. The karyotype is the number and type of chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Image of chromosomes arranged in pairs
All the genetic information of an organism

questions.explanation: The karyotype is a property of the organism; the karyogram is the image used to show it.

questions.prompt: Members of a species share the same genes but differ in some bases. What does this show?
options: Unity and diversity of genomes within a species
That the species is in the process of splitting
That each individual has a different set of genes
That mutation never occurs within a species
questions.explanation: Individuals share most of the genome (unity) but differ at a small number of positions such as SNPs (diversity). Different alleles, not different genes, cause variation.

questions.statement: Genome size is directly proportional to the complexity of an organism, so humans have the largest genome.
questions.explanation: Eukaryote genome sizes vary enormously and do not track complexity; some plants and amphibians have far larger genomes than humans, much of it non-coding DNA.

questions.text: A difference of a single base at one position between individuals is called a single-nucleotide ___.
questions.explanation: SNPs are the most common type of variation between individual genomes within a species.

questions.prompt: Which is a current or potential use of whole genome sequencing?
options: Changing the number of chromosomes in a patient
Personalised medicine based on an individual's genome
Producing karyograms without chromosomes
Determining an organism's age
questions.explanation: Sequencing whole genomes helps match treatments to individuals and is also used to investigate evolutionary relationships. Costs have fallen dramatically, so it is now widely used.

questions.prompt: In a karyogram, how could you tell the sex of a human?
options: Count the total number of chromosomes
Look at the longest chromosome pair
Look at the sex chromosomes: XX is female, XY is male
Check if chromosome 2 is fused
questions.explanation: Both sexes have 46 chromosomes; the sex chromosome pair differs, with females having two X and males an X and a smaller Y.

lessons.title: HL: Species concepts, keys and eDNA

questions.prompt: Why is the biological species concept difficult to apply to bacteria?
options: Bacteria cannot mutate
Bacteria reproduce asexually and exchange genes by horizontal gene transfer
Bacteria all have identical genomes
Bacteria have too many chromosomes
questions.explanation: The concept depends on interbreeding. Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission, and genes move between even distantly related bacteria, blurring species boundaries.

questions.statement: Horizontal gene transfer means genes passing from parent to offspring.
questions.explanation: That is vertical transfer. Horizontal gene transfer is movement of genes between organisms that are not parent and offspring, e.g. plasmid transfer between bacteria.

questions.text: Exchange of plasmids between bacteria is an example of ___ gene transfer.
questions.explanation: Plasmids carrying genes such as antibiotic resistance can pass between bacterial cells, including of different species.

questions.prompt: Why is chromosome number usually a shared trait of all members of a species?
options: Because chromosomes cannot mutate
Because all species have the same chromosome number
Because chromosome number is chosen by the environment
Because individuals with a different chromosome number usually cannot produce fertile offspring with the rest of the species
questions.explanation: Chromosomes must pair in meiosis. If numbers differ, pairing fails and offspring are usually infertile, so a change in chromosome number can isolate a population.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of using a dichotomous key to identify an organism.
items: Read the first pair of contrasting statements
Choose the statement that matches the organism
Follow the instruction to the next numbered pair
Repeat until the key gives a name
questions.explanation: Each step offers two choices; following matching choices narrows the possibilities until a single name is reached.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes a good choice for a pair of statements in a dichotomous key?
options: A clearly visible feature that does not vary with age, sex or season
The colour of the organism at a particular time of day
Whether the organism is rare
The behaviour of the organism when disturbed
questions.explanation: Good keys use stable, easily observed characteristics so that anyone can reliably make the same choice.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: DNA shed by organisms into water or soil
Short standard sequence that identifies a species
Series of paired choices leading to a name

questions.explanation: eDNA samples can be sequenced and matched against barcode databases to identify species present, complementing traditional keys.

questions.statement: Environmental DNA can reveal species in a habitat even if no individuals are seen or caught.
questions.explanation: Organisms shed cells, skin, mucus and waste. Sequencing DNA from a water or soil sample detects species from these traces, which is useful for rare or hidden species.

questions.prompt: How are species identified from an eDNA sample?
options: By growing the organisms from the DNA
By making a karyogram from the DNA
By sequencing barcode regions and comparing them with a database of known species' sequences
By measuring the total mass of DNA in the sample
questions.explanation: Barcode sequences differ between species, so matching sample sequences to a reference database identifies which species contributed DNA.

questions.text: A short, standardised DNA sequence used to identify species is called a DNA ___.
questions.explanation: Like a product barcode, it is a short sequence that is distinctive for each species.
